reconcile.note: Henry argues Deuteronomy condemns Moab's intent to curse Israel, which God overruled into a blessing rather than an actual curse taking effect.

discrepancy.note: Spinoza treats Balaam's cursing power as genuine, citing Deuteronomy's own claim that God had to change his curse into a blessing.

quotes.text: His speeches must certainly have had much weight with God, and His power for cursing must assuredly have been very great from the number of times that we find stated in Scripture, in proof of God's great mercy to the Jews, that God would not hear Balaam, and that He changed the cursing to blessing (see Deut. xxiii:6, Josh. xxiv:10, Neh. xiii:2).
quotes.attr: Benedict de Spinoza (d. 1677), A Theologico-Political Treatise, Part I, trans. R. H. M. Elwes (1883), ch. III, on Numbers 24:10 and Deuteronomy 23:4.

sides.snippet: I called you to curse my enemies, and, behold, you have altogether blessed them these three times.
sides.verseText: Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together; and Balak said to Balaam, I called you to curse my enemies, and, behold, you have altogether blessed them these three times.

sides.snippet: they hired against you Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse you
sides.verseText: because they didn't meet you with bread and with water in the way, when you came forth out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse you.
